idea: Learning from examples begins with a very ordinary problem: the rule we need is real, but too tangled to write down by hand. A teacher can show many finished lesson plans, therapy replies, table answers, ad pages, user searches, or tissue images, but cannot list every condition that makes each one right. The basic idea is to let a system try a rule, compare its answers with examples or chosen comparisons, and keep changing the rule until the mistakes become smaller. In COMA and the software-development agent paper, the examples are not just final answers, but traces of planning, checking, and revising. In BaiJia and coTherapist, the examples carry a style of speech and judgment that the system is meant to imitate without copying one fixed script. In graph, recommendation, and image papers, examples often come as pairs: these two cases should be treated as alike, and these two should be kept apart. The human need is the same across the group: reuse past cases without pretending that the next case will be an exact repeat. A simple lookup table fails because new buildings, emergency calls, user sequences, languages, chemicals, and shopping sessions arrive in forms the table has never seen. Learning is the controlled gamble that the examples contain a reusable shape hiding below their surface details. The danger is that the system may learn the wrong shape, such as a bias in who wrote an answer, a shortcut in a table layout, or a local pattern that fails in a new setting.
why: Learning works when past cases are not random scraps, but samples from a world with repeatable structure. If therapy replies that are useful share tone, timing, and clinical boundaries, then many examples can reveal those habits better than a hand-written checklist. If ads and trackers tend to leave traces in code and URLs, then a detector can learn those traces while still being checked against new pages. The reason comparison helps is that it asks a smaller question than full labeling: not what is the perfect name, but which things should move closer in treatment and which should move apart. That is why tissue segmentation, recommendation graphs, and user-sequence papers can learn from paired views or repaired examples instead of requiring an expert label for every piece. The method breaks when the examples cover only the easy corner of the world, when copied labels repeat old errors, or when an artificial damaged case is unlike a real failure. It also breaks when the target keeps changing, as in new search pages, unseen graphs, low-resource languages, or fresh online tracking tricks. The hidden bargain is coverage versus simplicity: the learned rule must be flexible enough to fit real variation, but restrained enough that it does not treat accidental detail as law.
math: The mathematical object is a rule with many adjustable settings, where each setting changes how an input is turned into an answer, score, label, plan, or generated response. The input might be a biography, a construction request, a table image, a graph node with neighbors, a user click sequence, or a small set of examples from a new room. The system produces something that can be checked: a character reply, a formal data request, a tissue region, a bot warning, a ranked item, or an emergency-call response. Learning defines what counts as wrong, such as choosing the wrong answer, separating similar cases, merging different cases, forgetting old classes, or drifting from good practice. The system then repeatedly changes its settings to reduce that wrongness on the available evidence. In comparison-based learning, the central measurement is nearness in behavior: two views of the same user intent, tissue type, or graph relation should lead to similar internal treatment, while mismatched cases should not. In semi-supervised graph work, unlabeled neighbors are used carefully because nearby nodes may carry clues, but the method must avoid turning uncertain guesses into false facts. In few-shot and domain-specific reranking work, the scarce resource is labeled data, so the math asks how much a rule can be adjusted from a few trusted examples before it overfits them. In federated visual primitive sharing, the scarce resource is communication and privacy, so devices share reusable visual pieces rather than all local detail. The principle is not magic imitation, but error-guided reuse under limits: keep the parts of past experience that help future cases, discard noise, and watch for settings where the past is a poor map.
family: These papers are siblings because they all face the same pressure: useful behavior is easier to demonstrate than to define completely. Lesson planning, role-play, construction data exchange, therapy support, search behavior, table question answering, and graph anomaly detection all require judgments that would become brittle if written as fixed rules. The repeated naive strategy is to build a checklist or a single prompt and hope every future case follows it. That fails because the real cases vary in wording, layout, culture, visual setting, user intent, graph shape, and hidden error patterns. The common move is to expose a system to examples, comparisons, weak labels, or simulated failures, then make it carry forward the reusable pattern rather than the surface copy. What changed in this family is the breadth of what counts as an example: not only labeled rows, but agent traces, eye movements, unlabeled graph neighbors, paired images and text, synthetic anomalies, reward-marked research chains, and human preference judgments. The family also shares a trust problem, because learned behavior is only as sound as the evidence and checks behind it. The central tradeoff is adaptation versus reliability: the system must change enough to fit a new classroom, clinic, language, graph, or store, but not so much that it forgets older knowledge or learns a convenient false shortcut.
dots: COMA, Lang2Plan, and the software-development agent paper treat learning as guided practice over workflows, where planning, acting, checking, and revising become part of what is learned. BaiJia and coTherapist show the same idea in human-facing language, where the desired output is not just correct content but a recognizable voice, role, or professional boundary. TabTune and domain-specific reranking focus on the plumbing of learning: make inputs comparable, run fair checks, and ask whether a small trusted set is enough to beat much larger but less targeted training. The graph papers use examples plus neighborhood structure, as in semi-supervised instruction tuning, One-for-All community search, SNBot, PAGE, and class-domain incremental learning. Their shared question is when nearby or damaged cases reveal truth, and when they merely spread mistakes. The recommendation papers RaDAR and adaptive sequential recommendation learn by creating altered views of user-item records, then checking whether the altered view still preserves the user's intent. Histopathology segmentation and multimodal retrieval connect pictures with text descriptions, using comparison to teach the system which visual regions or items belong with which meanings. AdVersa, SHIELD, and DeepResearch-9K use learned behavior under pressure, where the system must handle changing attacks, trainee mistakes, or long answer-finding chains rather than one clean label. The consent, search-behavior, eye-tracking, authorship-bias, and shopping-persona studies remind us that examples can come from people, and people bring literacy limits, attention patterns, identity, and ownership bias. Across all of them, learning is the act of turning observed cases into a rule for unseen cases while asking whether the observations are broad, honest, and checked enough to deserve trust.
picture: Imagine teaching a cook by giving recipes, tastings, corrections, and a few warnings about what went wrong in past kitchens. The cook is not memorizing every plate, but learning which choices usually travel well to a new pantry and which only worked because one ingredient or diner was unusual. Good learning keeps that transferable judgment while staying alert for the moment when the new kitchen is too different from the old lessons.
